chapter_title: Basic VR Interactions: Gaze, Raycasting, and Teleportation
chapter_summary:
Effective interaction is at the heart of any compelling VR experience. Unlike traditional flat-screen interfaces, VR demands intuitive and natural ways for users to engage with their virtual environment. Two fundamental interaction patterns you'll frequently encounter are gaze-based selection and raycasting, often complemented by locomotion systems like teleportation to navigate larger spaces comfortably. Gaze interaction, while simple, allows users to select or activate objects by simply looking at them for a specified duration. This is particularly useful in experiences where controllers might not be present or for very basic interactions. Implementing gaze typically involves attaching a script to the camera that casts a ray forward and detects hits on interactable objects, triggering an event after a certain dwell time.

Raycasting, on the other hand, provides a more precise and versatile interaction method, especially when controllers are available. Imagine a laser pointer extending from your virtual hand; that's essentially what a raycaster does. The XR Interaction Toolkit provides `XR Ray Interactor` components, which can be attached to your controller game objects (usually found under the `XR Origin`'s `LeftHand Controller` and `RightHand Controller`). These interactors project a ray into the scene, allowing users to point at and interact with objects from a distance. For an object to be interactable via raycasting, it typically needs an `XR Grab Interactable` or `XR Simple Interactable` component, along with a Collider. The ray interactor will highlight the object it's pointing at, providing crucial visual feedback to the user. Common mistakes here include forgetting to assign a `Line Renderer` to the `XR Ray Interactor` to visualize the ray, or not having colliders on the target objects. Also, ensure your ray interactor's "Interaction Layer Mask" is set correctly to interact with the desired layers.

Once users can interact with objects, they also need to move around the virtual world. While smooth locomotion (walking or flying) can be implemented, it's a common cause of motion sickness for many users, especially beginners. Teleportation offers a comfortable alternative, allowing users to instantly jump from one point to another. The XR Interaction Toolkit provides a robust teleportation system. This system typically involves three main components: a `Teleportation Provider`, `Teleportation Area`s, and `Teleportation Anchor`s. The `Teleportation Provider` (usually located on the `XR Origin`) manages the actual teleportation logic. `Teleportation Area` components define regions where the user can teleport to, often represented by a flat surface like a floor. `Teleportation Anchor` components are similar but allow teleportation to specific, fixed points, potentially with a specific orientation.

To set up teleportation, you'll first ensure your `XR Origin` has a `Teleportation Provider` component. Then, for any surface you want the player to be able to teleport onto, add a `Teleportation Area` component. This component requires a `Collider` (e.g., a `Box Collider` for a plane) to define its boundaries. For specific teleport points, add an `Teleportation Anchor` component. The `Teleportation Anchor` also has a "Teleportation Position" and "Teleportation Rotation" property, allowing you to fine-tune where the user lands and which way they face. The `XR Ray Interactor` on your controllers will automatically detect these `Teleportation Area`s and `Teleportation Anchor`s, displaying a valid teleportation reticle when pointing at them. Activating the teleport (e.g., by pressing a specific controller button) will then move the `XR Origin` to the target location. A common issue with teleportation is that the raycaster might not be hitting the teleportation areas, often due to incorrect layer masks on either the ray interactor or the teleportation area, or simply the area being too far away or behind other objects. Always ensure the "Interaction Layer Mask" on your `XR Ray Interactor` includes the layer your `Teleportation Area`s are on.

While the XR Interaction Toolkit provides excellent out-of-the-box solutions, you might sometimes need to implement custom interaction logic. For instance, a simple gaze-based interaction could involve a C# script. You could attach a script to your main camera that performs a `Physics.Raycast` every frame. If the ray hits an object with a specific tag (e.g., "GazeInteractable"), you can start a timer. If the timer reaches a certain duration, you trigger an interaction event on that object. This demonstrates how you can combine Unity's physics system with custom scripting to create unique interaction patterns. Remember that visual feedback is paramount in VR. When a user is gazing at an object, pointing with a ray, or selecting a teleportation destination, they need clear visual cues (e.g., highlighting, reticle changes) to understand what they are interacting with. Without this feedback, the experience can feel unresponsive and frustrating.

screens.title: Basic VR Interactions
screens.subtitle: Gaze, Raycasting, and Teleportation — building blocks for comfortable and intuitive VR

narration.text: In this chapter you’ll learn three foundational interaction systems for VR: gaze-based selection for simple no-controller experiences, raycasting for precise controller-driven pointing, and teleportation for comfortable locomotion. These techniques let users activate objects, pick up items from a distance, and move around without nausea. We’ll focus on the XR Interaction Toolkit mappings you’ll use most: XR Ray Interactor for controller rays, XR Grab or Simple Interactable for objects, and the Teleportation Provider with Teleportation Area and Teleportation Anchor for movement. You’ll also see a compact C# pattern for gaze detection using a physics raycast and a dwell timer, and how to combine visual feedback so users always know what they’re pointing at. Practical troubleshooting is integrated: common causes like missing colliders or mismatched interaction layer masks are explained so you can fix issues quickly. By the end you will be able to wire up controllers to point and grab, add teleportation spots correctly, and extend gaze and ray interactions with simple scripts. Think about an empty demo scene where a user points at a cube, the cube highlights, and a short press grabs it — that concrete interaction is what we’ll build toward. What interaction will you try first in your scene?

keyIdea.title: Why these interactions matter
keyIdea.text: Gaze gives minimal-device access, raycasting gives precision with controllers, and teleportation prevents motion sickness while enabling exploration.

First, you will identify and implement common VR interaction patterns such as gaze-based selection and controller raycasting. That skill matters because it determines how users select objects when controllers are unavailable or when precision pointing is required. Second, you will configure and use the XR Interaction Toolkit's locomotion components to add teleportation. You will learn which components belong on the XR Origin and which go on scene geometry, so teleport moves the user reliably. Third, you will learn to differentiate direct interactions—touching or grabbing—with indirect interactions—pointing at objects from a distance—so you choose the right affordance. screens.title: Gaze Interaction: Definition and Use Cases
screens.subtitle: Selecting by looking — when and why to use gaze in VR

narration.text: Gaze interaction is a lightweight VR selection method where the system detects where the user is looking and triggers an action after a dwell time. It is especially useful in experiences without controllers, on 360-video viewers, or in simple menus where pointing precision is not required. Mechanically, gaze commonly works by casting a ray from the camera forward each frame. When that ray hits an object tagged or flagged as gaze-interactable, a timer begins. If the timer reaches a preset dwell duration, an activation event fires. A concrete implementation you will build uses a script on the main camera to perform a Physics. Raycast each Update, check for a tag like "GazeInteractable", and increment a timer while the ray remains on the object. Visual feedback is critical: show a growing circular reticle, a progress bar, or a highlight so users know the dwell is advancing. A common misconception is that gaze replaces all other input; it does not. Gaze is great for minimal devices but is less precise than controller raycasting and not ideal for manipulating objects in 3D. Practice question: how long should your dwell be? Choose a value that balances speed and accidental activations, and test it with real users.

keyIdea.title: Gaze in brief
keyIdea.text: A camera-forward ray plus a dwell timer lets users select without controllers; visual feedback prevents accidental triggers.

content.html:
Core Concept
Gaze Interaction
Selecting items by looking at them for a short time.
Definition
A forward camera ray detects hits and a dwell timer triggers activation after a duration.
Why use gaze
  • Works without controllers — ideal for passive or simple experiences.
  • Low memory and input complexity for basic menus or 360 viewers.
  • Easy to implement with a camera-attached script and Physics.Raycast.
Concrete Example
Attach a camera script that casts a ray every frame, check for a "GazeInteractable" tag, increment a timer, and invoke the target's activation when the timer meets dwell time. Provide a circular progress reticle so users see the countdown.
Key Takeaway

Gaze is simple and accessible, but test dwell times and add strong visual feedback to avoid accidental activations.

Common Mistake

No visual progress indicator — users won’t know a selection is about to trigger and will perceive the app as unresponsive.

Gaze Implementation Sketch
// CameraGaze.cs (concept)
using UnityEngine;

public class CameraGaze : MonoBehaviour {
  public float dwellTime = 1.0f;
  float timer = 0f;
  GameObject current = null;

  void Update(){
    Ray ray = new Ray(transform.position, transform.forward);
    if(Physics.Raycast(ray, out RaycastHit hit)){
      if(hit.collider.gameObject.CompareTag("GazeInteractable")){
        if(current != hit.collider.gameObject){ timer = 0f; current = hit.collider.gameObject; }
        timer += Time.deltaTime;
        if(timer >= dwellTime){ current.SendMessage("OnGazeActivate"); timer = 0f; }
      } else { timer = 0f; current = null; }
    } else { timer = 0f; current = null; }
  }
}
This example shows the core claim, a concrete pattern, and a simple event call to activate the target. In practice add reticle visuals and test dwell length with users.

screens.title: Gaze vs Raycasting
screens.subtitle: When to use camera gaze, and when to use controller rays

narration.text: Gaze-based selection and raycasting are both ways to choose objects in VR, but they serve different needs. Gaze is a direct line from the user's head: it’s low-friction and perfect for minimal-device or passive viewing contexts. Use gaze for menus, simple hotspots, or accessibility scenarios. Raycasting from a controller is an indirect method: think of a laser pointer extending from a hand. It is more precise and flexible, enabling long-distance grabbing, pointing, and teleport targeting. A clear example: in a 360 photo viewer you might use gaze to open hotspots; in a manipulation-heavy scene where users pick up tools, controllers with XR Ray Interactor are the right choice. Common misconceptions include assuming gaze is always simpler to implement correctly; in fact, gaze needs careful dwell tuning and feedback to avoid frustration. Conversely, raycasting requires proper component setup—XR Ray Interactor, Line Renderer, reticle prefab, colliders, and Interaction Layer Mask—to be effective. The practical rule: choose gaze for simple selection without controllers, choose raycasting when precision and object manipulation matter. Gaze vs Raycasting means gaze = minimal input and menus; raycasting = precision, grabbing, and teleport targeting.. In practical terms, when to use camera gaze, and when to use controller rays. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Selection rule of thumb
keyIdea.text: Gaze = minimal input and menus; Raycasting = precision, grabbing, and teleport targeting.

content.html:
Comparison
Gaze
Camera-forward selection with dwell.
Pros
  • No controllers required.
  • Low input complexity for passive experiences.
Cons
  • Less precise for object manipulation.
  • Requires careful dwell timing and feedback.
Example
360 viewers where looking at a hotspot opens an info panel after a one-second dwell.
Comparison
Raycasting (Controller)
Laser-like pointer from a hand using XR Ray Interactor.
Pros
  • Precise pointing and grabbing at a distance.
  • Supports teleportation targeting and object highlights.
Cons
  • Requires controller hardware and component setup.
  • Needs visible line or reticle for good feedback.
Example
Right-hand XR Ray Interactor with Line Renderer and reticle prefab, used to grab an interactable cube and to select a teleport target on the floor.
Practical guidance
If your experience requires both simple menus and object manipulation, combine the patterns: use gaze for HUD or tutorial menus and raycasting for in-world object interaction. Always give visual cues for both methods.

screens.title: XR Ray Interactor: Components and Setup
screens.subtitle: Wiring controllers to ray interactors, line renderers, and reticles

narration.text: The XR Ray Interactor is the component that projects a ray from a controller and mediates distant interactions. In practice you attach an XR Ray Interactor to your LeftHand Controller and RightHand Controller objects under the XR Origin. To make the ray visible, add a Line Renderer component and assign a simple unlit material. You also set a reticle prefab — a small sphere or quad — so users can see where the ray intersects geometry. For objects to be recognized, they must have an interactable component such as XR Grab Interactable or XR Simple Interactable and they must include a Collider. The XR Ray Interactor exposes an Interaction Layer Mask; ensure the mask contains the layer assigned to your interactables and teleportation areas. A typical setup flow: expand XR Origin, attach XR Ray Interactor to both hand controller objects, add or verify Line Renderer, set the reticle prefab, and then check layer masks. A common mistake is forgetting the reticle or a material on the Line Renderer; the ray exists but users cannot see it, which makes the system feel broken. Always test in Play with a headset to confirm both visual and functional behavior.

keyIdea.title: XR Ray Interactor checklist
keyIdea.text: Attach to controllers, add Line Renderer + material, set reticle prefab, and validate Interaction Layer Mask and colliders.

content.html:
Process Flow
XR Ray Interactor Setup
Attach to controllers, add visual components, and align layers.
Step 1 — Attach
Put XR Ray Interactor on LeftHand and RightHand under XR Origin.
Step 2 — Make the ray visible
Add Line Renderer and assign a bright unlit material so the ray is visible in VR.
Step 3 — Reticle prefab
Set a small sphere or quad as the reticle so users see where they are pointing.
Step 4 — Interaction Layer Mask
Include layers used by interactables and teleport areas so the interactor can hit them.
Visual Checklist
  • Line Renderer present and assigned material.
  • Reticle prefab set and visible.
  • Controllers have XR Ray Interactor component attached.
  • Interaction Layer Mask includes interactable layers.
Example scenario
You add XR Ray Interactor to the right-hand controller, assign a green line material on the Line Renderer, and set a small sphere reticle prefab. You then point at an interactable cube and see the reticle and highlight before grabbing.
Pro tip
If the ray is visible but cannot hit objects, toggle the Interaction Layer Mask while watching the Inspector to find the correct layer combination.

screens.title: Interactable Objects: Colliders and Components
screens.subtitle: Why XR Grab Interactable and colliders are required for detection

narration.text: For rays or gaze to affect objects, the objects must be prepared correctly. An XR Grab Interactable or XR Simple Interactable component defines how an object responds to interaction, but the interactable alone is not enough — Unity relies on Colliders to detect hits. If you attach XR Grab Interactable to a GameObject without a Collider, the ray interactor or physics raycast has nothing to hit and the object will appear unresponsive. A concrete example: an Interactable Cube must have a Box Collider (or compatible collider) enabled on the same GameObject or a child. The collider’s bounds determine hit detection, so size and positioning matter; a tiny collider or one offset from a visible mesh will produce surprising misses. A common troubleshooting step is to toggle Gizmos in the Scene view and inspect the collider shape, then run the scene and point the ray — if no hit is registered, add or adjust the collider. Also ensure the object’s layer is included in the XR Ray Interactor’s Interaction Layer Mask. Remember: interactable component defines behavior, collider enables detection, and layer mask enables filtering.

keyIdea.title: Object readiness
keyIdea.text: Add collider + interactable component + correct layer to make an object detectable by rays and gaze.

content.html:
Definition
Interactable Objects
Combine a collider and an XR interactable component so rays and physics detect and trigger behavior.
Collider requirement
XR Grab Interactable needs a Collider on the same GameObject or a child so Physics.Raycast or XR Ray Interactor can register hits.
Collider sizing matters
A collider that is too small or offset will cause misses even when the mesh looks hittable. Adjust bounds in the Inspector and test with Gizmos on.
Layer mask check
If colliders are present but no interaction occurs, ensure the object's layer is included in the XR Ray Interactor's Interaction Layer Mask.
Scenario
You add XR Grab Interactable to a vase and forget the collider; the ray shows a reticle but the vase never highlights. Adding a Box Collider and re-testing immediately fixes the missing grabs.
Quick inspector checklist
  • Does the object have a Collider? (Box/Sphere/Mesh)
  • Is the Collider enabled and sized correctly?
  • Is the XR Grab Interactable or Simple Interactable present?
  • Is the object on a layer included by the interactor mask?
Common Mistake
Attaching the interactable only to a child object while the collider is on the parent without enabling the child — ensure colliders and interactable references align on the active GameObject tree.

screens.title: Teleportation: Concepts and Components
screens.subtitle: Provider, Area, and Anchor — how teleportation moves the XR Origin

narration.text: Teleportation in the XR Interaction Toolkit is a comfortable locomotion method that moves the XR Origin to a target location instantly, reducing motion sickness. The system is composed of three main parts. The Teleportation Provider, usually attached to the XR Origin, handles the actual movement logic. Teleportation Area components define regions—often flattened surfaces like the ground—where users are allowed to teleport. Teleportation Anchor components are fixed points that a user can teleport to, potentially with a prescribed rotation. The XR Ray Interactor on a controller recognizes these areas and anchors, showing a teleportation reticle when the target is valid. To set up teleportation: add a Teleportation Provider to the XR Origin, add Teleportation Area to ground planes with colliders, and add Teleportation Anchor to specific points. The XR Ray Interactor must include the layer your teleport objects are on in its Interaction Layer Mask so the ray can detect valid teleport targets. A common misconception is that attaching a Teleportation Area is enough; without the Teleportation Provider on the XR Origin, activating teleport has no effect. Always verify the Teleportation Provider is present and enabled.

keyIdea.title: Teleportation anatomy
keyIdea.text: Teleportation Provider moves the XR Origin; Area and Anchor define where users can land and face.

content.html:
Process Flow
Teleportation Components
How Provider, Area, and Anchor coordinate to move the XR Origin.
Teleportation Provider
Placed on XR Origin; executes the teleport and manages orientation when landing.
Teleportation Area
Attach to ground planes with an enabled Collider to allow area teleportation.
Teleportation Anchor
Place on specific points for fixed destinations; can define orientation on arrival.
Example Setup
Add Teleportation Provider to XR Origin, add Teleportation Area to the Ground plane with a Box Collider, and place Teleportation Anchors at fixed scenic viewpoints. Ensure the controllers' XR Ray Interactors include the ground's layer in their Interaction Layer Mask so the reticle appears when pointing at valid spots.
Troubleshooting
If teleport reticle does not appear while rays hit other objects, check the Interaction Layer Mask and confirm the Teleportation Area's Collider is enabled and not obscured by other geometry.
Key Takeaway

Teleportation requires both destination definition on geometry and an active Teleportation Provider on XR Origin to move the user.

screens.title: Step-by-step: Configure Ray Interactors and Teleportation
screens.subtitle: From XR Origin to ground plane — a checklist to run your scene

narration.text: Follow this step-by-step process to configure ray interactors and teleportation in a scene that already contains an XR Origin and a few cubes. First, expand the XR Origin and locate LeftHand Controller and RightHand Controller. Add or confirm an XR Ray Interactor component on both. Next, add a Line Renderer component and create a bright unlit material for the line so it appears clearly in VR. Assign the material to the Line Renderer and set a simple sphere prefab as the reticle in the XR Ray Interactor. Then, select the Ground plane and add a Teleportation Area component; ensure the Ground plane has an enabled Collider, like a Box Collider. For specific fixed points, add Teleportation Anchor components to empty GameObjects located where you want the user to land. Finally, make sure the Interaction Layer Mask on each XR Ray Interactor includes the layer your Ground plane and interactable objects are on. Test in Play with your headset; you should see rays, reticles, highlights, be able to grab cubes, and point to teleport destinations. If something fails, revisit layer masks and colliders first; they are the most common root causes.

keyIdea.title: Setup checklist
keyIdea.text: Add XR Ray Interactors, Line Renderers + reticle, Teleportation Provider on XR Origin, Teleportation Areas/Anchors with colliders, and align interaction layers.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Configure Ray Interactors & Teleportation
Follow the checklist and verify behavior in Play.
Step-by-step
  1. Add XR Ray Interactor to LeftHand and RightHand controllers.
  2. Add a Line Renderer and assign a bright unlit material so the ray is visible.
  3. Create a small sphere prefab and assign it as the reticle in the interactor.
  4. Add Teleportation Provider to the XR Origin if not present.
  5. Add Teleportation Area to the Ground plane and ensure an enabled Collider is present.
  6. Add Teleportation Anchors for fixed locations when desired.
  7. Set Interaction Layer Mask on the ray interactors to include the ground and interactable layers.
Example Test
Enter Play with a headset: you should see a ray from each hand, a reticle when pointing at surfaces, the cube highlight when pointing at an interactable, press the grab input to pick up the cube, and press the teleport input to move to a valid teleport reticle position.
If it fails
Check colliders first, then Interaction Layer Mask, then confirm the Teleportation Provider exists on the XR Origin.

screens.title: Custom Gaze Script Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: A compact C# pattern using Physics.Raycast and a dwell timer

narration.text: Sometimes you will want custom behavior that the XR Interaction Toolkit doesn't provide out of the box. A common case is a gaze script attached to the main camera that triggers events after a dwell duration. The pattern is straightforward: cast a Physics. Raycast from the camera each frame, detect whether the hit object qualifies as gaze-interactable, and increment a timer while the user continues looking at the same object. When the timer reaches the dwell threshold, call a method on the object, such as OnGazeActivate, to perform the action. The visual example included shows a simple CameraGaze script that checks for a tag like "GazeInteractable". Remember to reset the timer when the gaze leaves the object and to include visual feedback like a progress reticle so the user sees the countdown. A common misconception is that Update-based raycasts are too expensive; for simple scenes and single-camera checks this pattern is fine. If you need many simultaneous checks, consider more advanced optimizations. Final thought: keep activation idempotent — guard against multiple activations by resetting or disabling the gaze trigger after firing until some condition resets it.

keyIdea.title: Gaze script pattern
keyIdea.text: Raycast every frame, detect tag or component, accumulate dwell time, trigger activation and reset.

content.html:
Definition
Gaze Script Walkthrough
Implement a camera-attached script that detects gaze and fires activation after a dwell.
// CameraGaze.cs (illustrative)
using UnityEngine;

public class CameraGaze : MonoBehaviour {
  public float dwellTime = 1f;
  float timer = 0f;
  GameObject current = null;
  
  void Update(){
    Ray ray = new Ray(transform.position, transform.forward);
    if(Physics.Raycast(ray, out RaycastHit hit)){
      GameObject target = hit.collider.gameObject;
      if(target.CompareTag("GazeInteractable")){
        if(current != target){ timer = 0f; current = target; }
        timer += Time.deltaTime;
        if(timer >= dwellTime){ current.SendMessage("OnGazeActivate"); timer = 0f; }
      } else { timer = 0f; current = null; }
    } else { timer = 0f; current = null; }
  }
}
Notes
  • Use tags or a dedicated component to identify gaze targets.
  • Reset timers when gaze leaves to avoid false activations.
  • Add a progress reticle so users see the dwell advancing.
Concrete Example
Attach this script to the main camera, tag a cube with "GazeInteractable", and implement OnGazeActivate on the cube to perform the action. Test dwell time and reticle visibility to ensure a comfortable pace.
Key Takeaway

A short, Update-based raycast plus a dwell timer is a reliable and readable pattern for gaze activation in simple scenes.

screens.title: Common Issues: No Hits, No Teleport Reticle
screens.subtitle: How to diagnose missing interactions quickly

narration.text: When interactions appear broken, a small set of checks resolves most cases. If your ray is visible but cannot grab objects, first confirm the target has a Collider and an XR Grab Interactable or Simple Interactable component. Second, check the XR Ray Interactor’s Interaction Layer Mask — if the object’s layer is not included, the interactor will ignore it. Third, ensure the Line Renderer and reticle are assigned so users can see where they point; visual absence can be misinterpreted as functional failure. For teleportation-specific failures where other interactions still work, verify that Teleportation Area components exist on the ground and that their Colliders are enabled. Also check the Teleportation Provider is present on the XR Origin; without it, activating teleport does nothing. A concrete diagnostic: point at an object, look at the Inspector while pressing Play, and toggle the Interaction Layer Mask to see if the hit becomes active; if it does, you identified a mask issue. Another diagnostic is toggling Gizmos to display Collider bounds. These targeted checks save time and reduce guessing when an interaction does not behave as expected.

keyIdea.title: Diagnose quickly
keyIdea.text: Missing collider or wrong layer mask are the top causes; check colliders, masks, and the Teleportation Provider first.

content.html:
Troubleshooting
No Hits or No Reticle
A quick checklist to find the root cause and fix it fast.
Missing Collider
Ensure Collider exists and is enabled on the interactable object or its child.
Interaction Layer Mask
Confirm the interactor mask includes the target object's layer; mismatches are common.
Teleport Provider Missing
If teleport activation does not move the user, check for a Teleportation Provider on the XR Origin.
Visual Assets
Validate Line Renderer material and reticle prefab so users see the pointer and target markers.
Diagnostic Steps
  1. Enable Gizmos and inspect Colliders in Scene view.
  2. While in Play, toggle Interaction Layer Mask to find a working combination.
  3. Confirm Teleportation Provider exists and is enabled on XR Origin.
  4. Check for other geometry occluding the teleport area or blocking the ray.
Quick Fix
Adding or adjusting a collider and including the object's layer in the interactor mask resolves most “no hit” reports.

screens.title: Extending Interactions: Custom Logic and Feedback
screens.subtitle: Combining toolkit components with scripts to create polished interactions

narration.text: The XR Interaction Toolkit gives you solid defaults, but you will often extend or combine them with scripts to craft a polished experience. For instance, combine an XR Ray Interactor hit with a custom script on the target that responds to OnSelectEntered for grab logic and a custom highlight method when hovered. You can also use small scripts to modify reticle behavior: change the reticle color when pointing at a Teleportation Area versus pointing at an interactable object, or animate the Line Renderer width to provide depth cues. A practical example: a cube implements OnGazeActivate and OnSelectEntered—gaze opens its information panel, while the controller grab moves it. Another extension is to gate activation: after teleportation landings, disable gaze activation for a short grace period to prevent accidental triggers. A misconception is thinking toolkit components alone solve UX; visual feedback and small rules (grace periods, hold-to-grab, progress indicators) make interactions feel reliable and discoverable. Always test behavior combinations in Play and with a headset to validate the combined experience. content.html:
Extension
Custom Logic & Feedback
Combine toolkit components with scripts to refine behavior and visuals.
Example 1 — Dual activation
A cube responds to gaze by showing info and responds to grab to move. Use OnGazeActivate and XR grab callbacks together, ensuring they don’t conflict by gating one while the other is active.
Example 2 — Reticle context
Change reticle color or shape depending on whether the ray points at a Teleportation Area or an interactable, giving immediate context to the user’s action.
Design rule
Add short grace periods after teleportation and use progress indicators so activations are intentional and predictable.
Concrete pattern
Create a small manager script that listens to interactor hover and select events. On hover, call a highlight method on the target. On select, perform the action and optionally disable gaze activation for a short period to avoid accidental re-triggering immediately after teleport or a grab release.
Key Takeaway
Small scripts that coordinate feedback and gating are what make interactions feel polished; the toolkit provides hooks to do this cleanly.

screens.subtitle: Check understanding: diagnostics and expected fixes

narration.text: To assess your understanding, try diagnosing two common issues described in the chapter. First question: the ray is visible but the user cannot grab objects that have XR Grab Interactable. The correct diagnostic path checks for a missing Collider, then verifies the Interaction Layer Mask. Add or enable an appropriate Collider on the object and ensure the object’s layer is included in the interactor mask. Second question: teleportation reticle does not appear while grabbing works. Here the likely cause is that Teleportation Area colliders are on a layer excluded by the interactor's mask or the Teleportation Provider is missing on the XR Origin. The test is to inspect the Teleportation Area on the ground, confirm the Collider is enabled, and verify the provider exists. As you perform these checks, explain each step aloud: why a collider is needed, how mask filtering works, and what the Teleportation Provider does. This reflective practice solidifies the mental models and prepares you to debug similar interaction problems in larger scenes. Assessment Idea
Diagnostics and Fixes
Question 1
Ray visible but cannot grab objects with XR Grab Interactable. What to check?
  1. Is there an enabled Collider on the object?
  2. Is the object’s layer included in the Interaction Layer Mask of the ray interactor?
  3. Is the XR Grab Interactable attached to the active GameObject or a child with the collider?
Question 2
Teleport reticle not appearing while grabbing still works. Likely causes and fixes.
  1. Verify Teleportation Area exists on the ground and its Collider is enabled.
  2. Confirm the Teleportation Provider is present and active on XR Origin.
  3. Ensure the interactor mask includes the teleport layer.
Instructor tip
When you fix a reported issue, document the root cause and the exact inspector change you made. This habit speeds future debugging and teaches you the mappings between components and behavior.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to carry forward. First, gaze interaction is a camera-forward detection with a dwell timer that enables selection without controllers; always add clear visual feedback to indicate progress. Second, raycasting via XR Ray Interactor provides precision from controllers; attach Line Renderers, set a reticle prefab, and configure the Interaction Layer Mask so the interactor can detect your objects and teleport targets. Third, teleportation requires a Teleportation Provider on the XR Origin and Teleportation Area or Anchor components on scene geometry; colliders and layer masks must be aligned so the ray recognizes destinations. Keep these relationships in mind: interactable component defines behavior, collider enables detection, and layer masks filter which objects are hittable. These three pillars — gaze, raycast, and teleportation mapping — will let you design interactive, comfortable VR experiences. Use the checklist and hands-on steps from earlier screens to validate your scene quickly.

keyIdea.title: Three pillars
keyIdea.text: Gaze with dwell + feedback, XR Ray Interactor visibility + layers, Teleportation Provider + destinations and colliders.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Key Concepts
Key Concepts
Compact reminders of the chapter’s essential points.
Gaze Interaction
Look-to-select with a dwell timer and visible progress prevents accidental activations.
Raycasting
XR Ray Interactor projects a pointer from a controller; add Line Renderer and reticle for clarity.
Teleportation
Teleportation Provider moves XR Origin; Areas and Anchors mark valid destinations with colliders.
Summary
Remember the role mapping: Interactable = behavior, Collider = detection, Layer Mask = filtering. Verify these three to make interactions work reliably.

narration.text: As a final quick-reference, keep these practical reminders at hand while building VR interactions. First, always include visual feedback: reticles, highlights, and progress indicators tell the user what will happen when they act. Second, test with a headset early and often — what looks fine in the Editor may feel different in VR. Third, prioritize colliders and layer masks when debugging; they are the most frequent causes of failed hits or missing teleportation reticles. These short checks will save you time during iteration and give your users a clearer, more reliable experience. As you continue, practice wiring the XR Ray Interactor, adding colliders to interactables, and setting up Teleportation Areas. With those foundations in place you can customize visual feedback and add small scripts to refine behavior. Now, which diagnostic will you run first when something doesn’t respond in your scene?
